notes: Batch 3 (100 species), prepared by the coding agent on 2026-11-25/26 at the owner's request, for a portfolio project, with the same method as batch 2 (D-047). Sources read those days: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy (CC BY 4.0) via the GBIF API for names and classification; Wikidata (CC0) for the IUCN category, cited second-hand with the IUCN edition its statement references; English Wikipedia (one revision per species, recorded in each source) for range countries and seas, habitats, diet, threats and population figures, restated in our own words. IUCN pages were not read. Habitat and threat codes are our own lists (w-*), not the IUCN schemes. Countries and seas are those the article names in context; many lists are partial and say so in the geography citation note. Images from Wikimedia Commons, downloaded into catalogue/media: licence read from the Commons API at download time and compared with the file's embedded copyright fields; only CC0, public domain, CC BY and CC BY-SA files with a named creator. Trend is 'unknown' throughout.

editorial.overview: One of three orangutan species, living only in the north of the Indonesian island of Sumatra. It is rarer than the Bornean orangutan. Compared with its Bornean relative it eats more fruit and insects, and wild animals in the Suaq Balimbing swamp have been seen using sticks as tools. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly soft fruit, with more insects than the Bornean orangutan eats and less inner bark. It also takes bird eggs and small vertebrates, and uses stripped sticks to reach the seeds of spiny Neesia fruit.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as approximately 13,846 remaining in 2017. A 2016 survey had estimated 14,613 in the wild.

citations.note: Northern Sumatra only; in 2017 about 82.5% of the population was in Aceh Province.

editorial.overview: A gibbon found only on the Indonesian island of Java, in undisturbed rainforest up to about 2,450 m. Its coat is bluish-grey with a dark cap. Like all gibbons it has no tail and very long arms, and it moves through the trees by swinging from branch to branch during the day. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Fruit, leaves and flowers.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as fewer than 2,500 mature individuals in the wild. The article also gives fewer than 2,000 gibbons in eight viable sites.

citations.note: Endemic to Java.

editorial.overview: A gibbon of Southeast Asian forests, also called the white-handed gibbon. It travels by swinging under branches with its arms and is rarely found above 1,200 m. Its range once reached from southwest China through Thailand and Myanmar to the Malay Peninsula and northern Sumatra, and the mainland range has shrunk and broken up in recent decades. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly fruit (about half the diet, especially figs and other small sweet fruits), with young leaves, insects and flowers making up the rest.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Countries as listed in the article's range section. The Chinese subspecies (Yunnan) is described as possibly extinct.

editorial.overview: An Old World monkey found only in temperate mountain forests of central and southwest China, at 1,500 to 3,400 m. Adult males have long golden hair on the back and shoulders. Three subspecies live in Sichuan, Gansu, Shaanxi and Hubei, separated by densely settled valleys. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A plant eater whose main food is lichen, followed by young leaves, fruit and seeds, buds, mature leaves, herbs, bark and flowers. The mix changes markedly with the seasons.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as some 10,000 individuals from estimates made between 1995 and 2006; elsewhere the article gives 8,000 to 15,000.

citations.note: Endemic to central and southwest China. Zoos abroad are not counted.

editorial.overview: A medium-sized lemur of Madagascar, also called the white sifaka. It lives in groups of about 2 to 13 animals in habitats from rainforest to the dry deciduous forests of the west and the spiny thickets of the south, and probably still has the largest range of any sifaka. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A plant eater: mostly leaves, especially in the dry season, along with fruit, bark and flowers. It seems to pick food for quality (low tannin) rather than availability, and forages mainly in the morning and late afternoon.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Endemic to Madagascar (west and south).

media.altText: A Verreaux's sifaka with a white face eating a leaf

editorial.overview: A nocturnal lemur of Madagascar with rodent-like teeth that never stop growing and a thin, flexible middle finger. It taps on wood and listens for hollows where grubs live, gnaws a hole and pulls the larvae out. It lives mainly on the island's east coast and spends almost all its time in the trees. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore: seeds, nuts, fruit, nectar, plant sap and fungi, plus wood-boring insect larvae and honey. It forages for up to 80% of the night.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Endemic to Madagascar, mainly the east coast. The captive breeding centre in the USA is not counted.

media.altText: An aye-aye with large eyes and ears on a branch

editorial.overview: One of two ruffed lemurs, both found only on Madagascar. It spends most of its time high in the canopy of the seasonal rainforests on the island's east side, preferring tall, mature forest deep inside unbroken blocks. Its range is larger than the red ruffed lemur's but its population is much smaller. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: The most fruit-dependent of all lemurs: fruit makes up about 92% of the wild diet, with nectar, flowers, leaves and some seeds. Groups use 19 to 40 tree species for food depending on the site.

population.note: The source gives densities at study sites but no total population.

citations.note: Endemic to the eastern rainforests of Madagascar. Captive-born animals released from the USA are not counted as a range.

media.altText: A black-and-white ruffed lemur with a white ruff of fur on a branch

editorial.overview: A small, bright orange New World monkey found only in the Atlantic coastal forest of Brazil's Rio de Janeiro state. Most of its original forest was cleared, and it now lives in forest fragments, reserves and private land. Reintroduction of zoo-born animals, translocations and replanting have helped its numbers grow. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly ripe fruit and small animal prey, with smaller amounts of nectar and tree gum. One study recorded 160 plant species eaten, though seven of them made up over half of plant feeding.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: A 2022/2023 census estimated about 4,800 in the main area, plus smaller unknown numbers in coastal forest.

citations.note: Endemic to the Atlantic Forest of Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil.

editorial.overview: One of the smallest primates, weighing under half a kilogram, recognised by its long white crest of hair. It lives in tropical forest edges and secondary forest in a small area of northwest Colombia. Before 1976 up to 40,000 were caught and exported for biomedical research. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: About 40% fruit and 40% animal food, mainly insects caught by stealth, pouncing, chasing and searching holes and leaves, plus plant gum. It eats small seeds and spreads them through the forest.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Wild population estimated at 6,000 individuals, of which 2,000 adults.

citations.note: Restricted to northwest Colombia, between the Atrato River, the Cauca and Magdalena rivers and the Atlantic coast to the north.

media.altText: A cotton-top tamarin with a crest of white hair

editorial.overview: A large spider monkey of Central America and southern and eastern Mexico. It lives high in rainforest, semi-deciduous and mangrove forest, and can hang by its tail while it feeds. Groups of 20 to 42 split into smaller parties to forage by day. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly ripe fruit, which it searches for over large areas of forest.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Central America from Panama to Mexico, as the article lists. It may also occur in a small part of Colombia.

media.altText: A Geoffroy's spider monkey hanging from a branch by its long limbs

editorial.overview: A large Old World monkey of west central Africa and one of the most colourful mammals, with red and blue skin on the face and rump. Males are much larger than females. Hordes in Lopé National Park average about 620 animals, possibly the largest stable groups of wild primates. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore. Fruit and seeds are its favourite foods, but it also eats leaves, pith, mushrooms and animals from insects up to young duikers. In Lopé the diet was about half fruit and a quarter seeds.

population.note: Total population unknown; suspected to have fallen by more than 30% over 24 years.

citations.note: Between the Sanaga River and the Ogooué and Ivindo rivers. Gabon is its stronghold; it is not on Bioko Island.

media.altText: A mandrill showing its red and blue rump

editorial.overview: A nocturnal primate of Indonesia, the Malay Peninsula, southern Thailand and Singapore. It rests by day in tree forks and can defend itself with a bite and toxic saliva spread on its fur. It is one of the most common primates sold in Southeast Asian pet markets. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly tree sap, flower nectar and fruit, plus insects and other arthropods. It also takes snails and birds' eggs.

population.note: Population size unknown, as stated in the source.

citations.note: Sumatra and nearby islands, the Malay Peninsula and southern Thailand. Singapore is too small for our map.

media.altText: A Sunda slow loris with large eyes on a branch

editorial.overview: A large one-horned rhinoceros of the Indian subcontinent. It once ranged along the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra basins from Pakistan to the Myanmar border. Hunting and farming shrank that range, and today it lives in about 12 protected areas in the alluvial grasslands of northern India and southern Nepal. Protection has let its numbers grow from under 1,900 in the early 1990s. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A grazer that eats almost only grass, plus leaves, twigs and branches of shrubs and trees, flowers, fruit and water plants. It feeds in the mornings and evenings.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Estimated at 4,075 individuals as of March 2025.

citations.note: India and Nepal hold the living population. Bhutan has no permanent population; animals sometimes cross from India. Former range in Pakistan and Bangladesh is shown as extinct.

media.altText: An Indian rhinoceros and its calf, with folded armour-like skin, in grass

editorial.overview: A one-horned rhinoceros that once lived from eastern India through mainland Southeast Asia to Sumatra and Java. Poaching for its horn, colonial trophy hunting and habitat loss wiped it out almost everywhere. It now survives only in Ujung Kulon National Park on the western tip of Java; the last animal in Vietnam was shot in 2010. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A browser that eats shoots, twigs, young leaves and fallen fruit from many plants. It knocks down saplings and grabs food with its pointed, grasping upper lip.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as fewer than 100 individuals surviving in Ujung Kulon National Park.

citations.note: Living population only in Ujung Kulon, Java (Indonesia). Countries of the historical range named in the article are shown as extinct; the Vietnam population ended in 2010 and the Malay Peninsula one by 1932.

media.altText: A historical black-and-white photo of a Javan rhinoceros in an enclosure

editorial.overview: The largest living rhinoceros, with a broad, square mouth for grazing; it is also the most social rhino, living in groups of up to 14. Almost all wild animals belong to the southern subspecies, with South Africa as its stronghold. The northern subspecies is functionally extinct: its last known male died in Kenya in 2018. It is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A grazer of grassland and savanna, cropping grass with its wide, straight lips.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Southern white rhinoceros in the wild at the end of 2023. The northern subspecies survives only as a few captive animals.

citations.note: South Africa is the stronghold. Reintroduced within the former range in Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Uganda and Eswatini; a small population survives in Mozambique; introduced to Kenya and Zambia.

media.altText: A white rhinoceros standing on open grassland

editorial.overview: The largest wild equid and the most threatened zebra, with narrow stripes and a mule-like build. It lives in semi-arid savanna and bushland in parts of Kenya and Ethiopia and can go up to five days without water. Its numbers fell from about 15,000 in the 1970s to around 2,000 to 2,500. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Grasses, legumes and other herbs, and browse such as acacia when grass is scarce. Its hindgut digestion lets it live on poorer food than cattle and antelope need.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Wild numbers estimated at around 2,250 animals as of 2020.

citations.note: Kenya and Ethiopia. Extirpated from Somalia and Djibouti; status in South Sudan uncertain.

media.altText: Grévy's zebras with narrow black stripes in dry scrub

editorial.overview: A small buffalo found only on the island of Mindoro in the Philippines, and the country's only endemic wild cattle. It once lived across the island from the coast to over 2,000 m, but hunting and habitat loss have pushed it into a few remote grassy areas. Some animals now feed at night to avoid people. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A grazer of grasses and young bamboo shoots, preferring cogon grass and wild sugarcane.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Current wild estimates place the population at 30 to 200 individuals. It was about 10,000 in the early 1900s.

citations.note: Endemic to Mindoro, Philippines.

media.altText: A tamaraw, a small dark buffalo with short V-shaped horns

editorial.overview: An antelope of the Eurasian steppe with a large, drooping nose. Huge herds graze semi-desert, steppe and grassland, now mainly in Kazakhstan and the Kalmykia and Astrakhan regions of Russia, with a separate subspecies in Mongolia. Numbers fell by up to 95% in the 2000s and mass die-offs struck in 2015, but anti-poaching work and new protected areas have brought a strong recovery. It is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Grazes many kinds of plants in semi-desert and steppe, including some that are poisonous to other animals. Deep snow and harsh winds in winter can stop it reaching grass.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Global estimate as of December 2023. Later counts reported 3.9 million adults in Kazakhstan alone in spring 2025.

citations.note: Kazakhstan, Russia (Kalmykia and Astrakhan) and Mongolia. Part of the Ustyurt population winters in Uzbekistan and sometimes Turkmenistan. Regionally extinct in Romania, Ukraine, Moldova and China.

media.altText: A male saiga antelope with ringed horns wading through shallow water

editorial.overview: A pale desert antelope with long, spiral horns, the only member of its genus. Once common across the Sahara, it survives in the wild mainly between Niger, Chad and Mauritania and has been reintroduced to Morocco and Tunisia. It can live almost indefinitely without drinking, taking water from plants and dew. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Grasses and the leaves of shrubs, leguminous herbs and bushes. Its long digestion suits tough grasses and saves water.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Fewer than 500 are thought to exist in the wild, mostly in Niger, Chad and Mauritania.

citations.note: Wild in Niger, Chad and Mauritania; reintroduced to Morocco and Tunisia. Locally extinct in Western Sahara, Algeria, Libya, Egypt and Sudan. Rare nomads may still reach Algeria and Libya.

media.altText: Addax antelopes with long spiral horns, adults and young

editorial.overview: A white desert antelope with long, curved horns that once lived in a strip of steppe and semi-desert across north Africa. Hunting wiped it out in the wild, and it was listed as Extinct in the Wild in 2000. Captive-bred herds released in Chad's Ouadi Rimé-Ouadi Achim reserve from 2016 led to its downlisting to Endangered in 2023. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A grazer that gets most of its water from plants: grasses, herbs, shrubs, succulents, legumes, roots, buds and fruit. In the dry season it eats acacia seedpods and perennial grasses.

population.note: No current wild total in the source; it gives a small reintroduced herd in Chad.

citations.note: Reintroduced to the wild in Chad. The other countries are those the article says IUCN lists it as extirpated from; herds kept in fenced reserves (Tunisia, Morocco, Senegal) and ranches are not counted.

media.altText: A scimitar oryx with long backward-curving horns

editorial.overview: The only living big cat of the genus Panthera in the Americas, with a tan coat covered in dark rosettes. Its range runs from the southwestern United States through Mexico and Central America to the Amazon, Paraguay and northern Argentina, though it has shrunk greatly. Its very strong bite lets it pierce turtle shells and kill mammals by biting through the skull. It is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An obligate carnivore. Prey ranges from 1 to 130 kg, with capybara and giant anteater the most selected, plus deer, peccaries, agoutis, caimans, anacondas, turtles and, in the Pantanal, fish. It also takes cattle where wild prey is scarce.

population.note: No global population figure in the source; the wild population is thought to have declined since the late 1990s.

citations.note: Countries as listed in the article's present range; French Guiana is not on our map. Locally extinct in El Salvador and Uruguay.

media.altText: A jaguar with a spotted golden coat resting in a tree

editorial.overview: A wild cat with large dusky-grey blotches that look like clouds. It lives in dense forest from the Himalayan foothills to mainland Southeast Asia and southern China. A skilled climber, it can descend tree trunks head first, rests in trees by day and hunts on the forest floor at night. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Stalks or ambushes both tree-dwelling and ground-dwelling vertebrates. Prey recorded in Thailand includes macaques, hog deer and porcupines.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Thought to be declining, with fewer than 10,000 adults and no more than 1,000 in any subpopulation.

citations.note: From Nepal, Bhutan and India to Myanmar, Bangladesh, Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia and southern China, with records in Laos and Cambodia. Locally extinct in Taiwan and Singapore, and possibly in Vietnam.

media.altText: A clouded leopard with large cloud-shaped markings

editorial.overview: A medium-sized wild cat found only on the Iberian Peninsula. Overhunting, habitat loss and the crash of rabbit populations brought it to the edge of extinction, with only 94 left in two Andalusian populations in 2002. Habitat work, rabbit restocking, captive breeding and reintroductions have since brought it back to more than 2,000 animals. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A rabbit specialist: European rabbits make up about 75% of its food, supplemented by red-legged partridges, rodents and occasionally young deer, mouflon and ducks. A male needs about one rabbit a day.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: 2,401 counted in 2024: 2,047 in Spain and 354 in Portugal.

citations.note: Spain and Portugal.

media.altText: An Iberian lynx with ear tufts and a spotted coat

editorial.overview: A small wild cat with short reddish-brown fur, a long flattened head and small rounded ears. It lives in lowland rainforest wetlands, especially swamp and peat-swamp forest near rivers, in southern Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo. Most records come from within 3 km of water. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly fish, plus frogs and probably crustaceans. Its teeth and strong jaws grip slippery prey, and captive cats readily plunge their heads underwater to catch live fish.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Southern Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo. Brunei is part of Borneo but the article does not name it, so it is marked uncertain.

media.altText: A flat-headed cat with reddish-brown fur and a long, flat head

editorial.overview: A reddish wild dog of South, East and Southeast Asia and the only member of its genus. It is very social, living in clans of about 12 and sometimes over 40, and hunts by day in packs. Once spread across much of Asia, it is now extinct in Central Asia and parts of Southeast Asia and survives in fragmented populations. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A pack hunter that prefers medium and large hoofed mammals. In tropical forests it overlaps in prey with tigers and leopards.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Populations decreasing and estimated at fewer than 2,500 mature individuals.

citations.note: Current records named in the article for India, Myanmar, Thailand, the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Java, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Laos, Cambodia and Yunnan (China). Possibly extinct in Vietnam and Russia; uncertain in North Korea and Pakistan; gone from Central Asia.

media.altText: A dhole, a rust-red wild dog with a dark bushy tail

editorial.overview: The largest canid of South America, with very long legs, large ears and a black mane it can raise. It lives alone rather than in packs, in grasslands with scattered bushes and trees, mostly in Brazil's Cerrado. It hunts at dusk, tapping the ground to flush prey, and spreads the seeds of the fruit it eats. It is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore whose main food is plant matter, especially the tomato-like wolf apple (40 to 90% of the diet), plus sugarcane, tubers and roots. It also catches rodents, rabbits, birds and eggs, reptiles, fish, snails and insects; over 300 food items are recorded.

population.note: No wild population figure in the source.

citations.note: Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Peru and Paraguay; almost locally extinct in Uruguay.

media.altText: A maned wolf with long legs and reddish fur in grassland

editorial.overview: A bear of Southeast Asian forests with the shortest fur of any bear and a pale chest patch it shows when threatened. It lives in tropical forests from northeastern India through mainland Southeast Asia to Borneo and Sumatra, mostly at low altitude, and does not hibernate. Its numbers are estimated to have fallen by 35% since the 1990s. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore: ants, bees, beetles, termites and honey, which it reaches with a very long tongue, plus seeds and many kinds of fruit. Birds and deer are eaten occasionally.

population.note: No population total in the source; it is estimated to have declined by 35% since the 1990s.

citations.note: Countries as listed in the article, from northeastern India to Brunei, Indonesia and Malaysia.

media.altText: A sun bear with short black fur and a pale chest patch

editorial.overview: The only bear native to South America, living along the Andes from Venezuela to northwestern Argentina. Pale markings around the eyes give it its name. It uses cloud forest, high grassland (páramo), dry forest and scrub, but its best habitat is humid mountain forest, and its populations have become fragmented over the last 500 years. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: More plant-eating than most bears, with meat only about 5 to 7% of the diet. Common foods are cacti, bromeliads, orchid bulbs, fallen fruit, palm hearts and moss, and it climbs trees to reach ripe fruit.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Andes of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, western Bolivia and northwestern Argentina.

media.altText: A spectacled bear with pale markings on its face

editorial.overview: A shaggy bear of the Indian subcontinent that has evolved to eat ants and termites. It lives in moist and dry tropical forest, savanna, scrub and grassland below 1,500 m. People have reduced its habitat and hunted it for food and body parts. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Termites, ants and bees, found by smell: it digs into mounds and sucks the insects up through its muzzle with a noise that carries 180 m. It also eats fruit, other plants and carrion.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Fewer than 20,000 are estimated to survive in the Indian subcontinent and Sri Lanka.

citations.note: India, the Terai of Nepal, Bhutan and Sri Lanka. Regionally extinct in Bangladesh.

media.altText: A sloth bear walking along a dirt track

editorial.overview: A medium-sized black bear of Asia with a pale V-shaped patch on its chest, also called the moon bear. It occurs patchily from southeastern Iran through the Himalayas to mainland Southeast Asia, China, Taiwan, Korea, the Russian Far East and Japan. A good climber, it bends branches into nest-like platforms when feeding in trees. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly plants but omnivorous: fruit, nuts, acorns, seeds, honey, grasses, bark, roots and mushrooms, plus insects and their larvae, termites, eggs and carrion.

population.note: No global population figure in the source.

citations.note: Patchy range as described in the article, from Iran to Japan; mainland Southeast Asia except Malaysia. South Korea and Japan hold small remnant populations.

media.altText: An Asian black bear foraging among plants

editorial.overview: A slender, long-tailed, cat-like carnivore found only on Madagascar, and the island's largest mammalian predator. It has evolved many cat-like features, such as retractable claws, but belongs to a family of its own with Madagascar's other carnivores. It lives only in forest, at low density across the island, and hunts by day and night. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: More than half its prey are lemurs; it also takes tenrecs, rodents, lizards and birds. In the western dry forest over 90% of its prey were vertebrates.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Total within protected areas estimated at about 2,500; numbers outside them are not given.

citations.note: Endemic to Madagascar, in remaining forest across the island.

media.altText: A fossa, a slender cat-like animal with a long tail

editorial.overview: A mink-sized weasel of the North American prairies that depends on prairie dogs for food and shelter. It declined through the 20th century as prairie dogs were poisoned and sylvatic plague spread, and was declared extinct in 1979. A small wild population found in Wyoming in 1981 founded a captive-breeding programme that has reintroduced it to eight US states, Canada and Mexico. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Prairie dogs make up to 90% of its diet; it hunts them at night, often while they sleep in their burrows.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: About 300 individuals in wild populations as of 2026, four of them self-sustaining.

citations.note: Reintroduced across eight western US states, Canada and Mexico; self-sustaining wild populations are in South Dakota, Arizona and Wyoming.

media.altText: A black-footed ferret with a dark mask and black legs

editorial.overview: One of the rarest seals, surviving in small, isolated groups in the eastern Mediterranean, especially the Aegean, and on the Atlantic coast of Madeira and Cabo Blanco in West Africa. Centuries of hunting and, later, persecution by fishermen drove it from most of its range. Mothers now give birth in hard-to-reach sea caves rather than on open beaches. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Fish, crustaceans and molluscs, mainly octopus, squid, lobsters, mullets, flatfish, tuna, sardines and eels. It feeds by day, mostly in shallow water but down to 250 m, and has been seen lifting rocks to find prey.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Estimated 800 to 1,000 individuals as of 2026 in isolated subpopulations.

citations.note: Mediterranean coasts of Croatia, Cyprus, Greece, Albania and Turkey, and the Atlantic off Madeira (Portugal), Mauritania and Western Sahara. Possibly extirpated around Egypt, Italy, Libya, Montenegro and Tunisia (and France, Malta and southern Spain); status unknown in Algeria, Israel, Lebanon, Morocco and Syria.

media.altText: A Mediterranean monk seal resting on a pebble beach

editorial.overview: A large, slow aquatic mammal of warm coasts, rivers and estuaries from the eastern United States to northern Brazil. It has two subspecies: the Florida manatee and the Antillean manatee of the Caribbean. Collisions with boats are a major danger, and red tides have killed many. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A strict plant eater that grazes over 60 kinds of aquatic plants in fresh and salt water for four to eight hours a day. Its teeth are replaced continuously from the back, like a conveyor belt.

population.note: No range-wide total in the source; it gives partial and uncertain counts for some subpopulations.

citations.note: United States (Florida) and the countries the article lists for the Antillean manatee, plus northern Brazil; French Guiana and Curaçao are not on our map. Presence in Haiti is uncertain.

media.altText: A West Indian manatee mother and calf swimming underwater

editorial.overview: A marine mammal related to manatees and the only strictly sea-living plant-eating mammal. It lives in shallow coastal waters with seagrass meadows across the Indo-West Pacific, in the waters of some 40 countries. Northern Australia is its stronghold; elsewhere many populations are small, fragmented and close to disappearing. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly seagrass, especially of the genera Halophila and Halodule, grazed from the seabed with its down-turned snout and muscular upper lip.

population.note: No global total in the source; it gives regional figures (e.g. over 10,000 in Shark Bay, over 25,000 in the Torres Strait) and a 20% worldwide decline over 90 years.

citations.note: Countries and seas the article names with current populations; it lives in the waters of about 40 countries, so this list is partial. Gone from Taiwan, Hong Kong and Mauritius; in Japan only a tiny population near Okinawa.

media.altText: A dugong swimming over seagrass

editorial.overview: A baleen whale and the second-longest animal after the blue whale. It lives in all the major oceans from polar to tropical waters, absent only near the pack ice and in a few small seas. Decades of whaling cut its numbers sharply; the North Atlantic population is considered fully recovered, while others are still recovering. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Small schooling fish, small squid and crustaceans such as krill and copepods. It sometimes circles a school at speed to bunch the fish, then rolls on its side to engulf them.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Global estimate as of 2018.

citations.note: Worldwide in the major oceans; seas named in the article are added. Country waters are not listed.

media.altText: A fin whale at the surface, seen from above, with its blow

editorial.overview: The largest toothed whale and the largest toothed predator, with a huge square head holding the spermaceti organ. It lives in deep water worldwide and dives for long periods to hunt by echolocation. Commercial whaling from the 18th century reduced a population once estimated at 1.1 million. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly squid, crushed in a muscular first stomach chamber; thousands of undigested squid beaks can build up in the stomach. It also eats fish, including deep-sea sharks.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Total unknown; estimated at as many as 360,000 worldwide.

citations.note: Worldwide in the open ocean, including the Mediterranean but not the Black Sea; presence in the Red Sea uncertain.

media.altText: A sperm whale mother and calf swimming underwater

editorial.overview: A freshwater dolphin of the Ganges and related rivers in India, Nepal and Bangladesh. It is effectively blind and finds its way and its prey by echolocation in the murky water. It is India's national aquatic animal. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Prawns and other crustaceans and fish such as carp and mahseer, found by echolocation.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: A 2025 survey counted 6,324 in India. Figures for Nepal and Bangladesh are not included.

citations.note: India, Nepal and Bangladesh.

media.altText: A Ganges river dolphin breaking the water surface

editorial.overview: A blunt-headed dolphin that lives in scattered groups near coasts and in estuaries and rivers of South and Southeast Asia, from the Bay of Bengal to New Guinea and the Philippines. It can squirt jets of water up to 1.5 m, and in some places it has a long tradition of cooperative fishing with people. Small river populations remain in the Mekong, Ayeyarwady and Mahakam. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Bony fish such as catfish, fish eggs, squid, octopus, cuttlefish and crustaceans. Groups circle and trap prey just below the surface.

population.note: No global total in the source; it lists small subpopulation counts (e.g. about 105 in the Cambodian Mekong in 2024).

citations.note: Coasts, estuaries and rivers as named in the article; presence in Chinese and Taiwanese waters is doubtful and not shown.

media.altText: Irrawaddy dolphins surfacing in a river

editorial.overview: The largest of the four living anteaters, with a long snout, a bushy tail and powerful front claws. It ranges from Honduras to Bolivia and northern Argentina, foraging in open grassland and resting in forest. It has disappeared from several countries, and its total population fell by more than 30% over three generations. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly ants and termites, dug out with its front claws and collected with a long, sticky tongue.

population.note: No population total in the source; it fell by more than 30% over three generations to 2014.

citations.note: From Honduras to Bolivia and northern Argentina, using the countries the article names; the Guianas are also named as range but not by country, so they are left out. Extirpated in Uruguay, Belize, El Salvador and Guatemala, and in parts of Costa Rica, Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay.

media.altText: A giant anteater with a long snout and bushy tail walking on the ground

editorial.overview: The largest living armadillo, found east of the Andes across much of northern South America and south to northern Argentina. It is solitary and nocturnal and digs very large burrows, which dozens of other species also use. Its numbers may have fallen by 30 to 50% over three decades. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly termites, often eating a whole mound's colony, plus ants, worms, spiders and other invertebrates, small vertebrates and carrion. It rips mounds open with its huge front claws.

population.note: No population figure in the source; it may have declined by 30 to 50% over three decades.

citations.note: East of the Andes to northern Argentina, absent from eastern Brazil and eastern Paraguay. Countries are those the article names; the list is partial.

media.altText: A giant armadillo with an armoured shell among plants

editorial.overview: A scaly, ant-eating mammal of the northern Indian subcontinent, northern Southeast Asia, southern China and Taiwan. It digs long burrows and rolls into a ball when threatened. Poaching for the illegal wildlife trade has cut its wild population by more than 80% over three generations. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly ants and termites, plus other invertebrates such as bee larvae, flies, worms and earthworms.

population.note: No population figure in the source; it is estimated to have declined by more than 80% over three generations.

citations.note: Southern Nepal, northeast India, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, northern Indochina (shown as Laos and Vietnam), southern China including Hainan, and Taiwan.

media.altText: A Chinese pangolin covered in brown scales

editorial.overview: A small possum found mainly in pockets of mountain ash, alpine ash and snow gum forest in the Central Highlands of Victoria, Australia. Thought extinct for decades, it was rediscovered in 1961. It needs old hollow trees for nesting and younger regrowth for food, and clearfell and salvage logging are its greatest threats. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore: wattle sap and gum, sugary lerps and many insects and other arthropods found under loose eucalypt bark. It forages at dusk in the sub-canopy, leaping from tree to tree.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as having halved to around 2,000 since the 1980s, before the 2009 Black Saturday fires.

citations.note: Central Highlands of Victoria, Australia. A single camera-trap record from Kosciuszko National Park (New South Wales) was reported in 2025.

media.altText: A small Leadbeater's possum on a branch

editorial.overview: An elephant of the humid tropical forests of West Africa and the Congo Basin, smaller than the savanna elephant. Families of up to 20 cows and young live together. By carrying seeds in its dung for several kilometres it helps keep the rainforest diverse. Poaching for ivory has driven a steep decline, estimated at around 86% in Central Africa over 31 years. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A plant eater: leaves, seeds, fruit and bark from at least 96 plant species; in Lopé National Park it ate at least 72 kinds of fruit. It visits mineral licks for salts.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: By 2013 fewer than 30,000 were estimated to remain.

citations.note: Central African rainforest from Cameroon to the DR Congo (largest stable population in Gabon), and the Upper Guinean forests of Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. Other range countries are not named in the article.

media.altText: An African forest elephant and calf at a forest pool

editorial.overview: A large wild bovine of Europe, also called the wisent. It was hunted to extinction in the wild in the early 20th century, when only 48 survived in zoos. Captive breeding, centred on Poland's Białowieża Forest, has allowed it to be reintroduced across Europe, and its numbers grow by about 15 to 18% a year. It is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly grasses, sedges and herbs, but it browses more than the American bison: shoots, twigs, bark and leaves of trees and shrubs.

population.note: No world total in the source; Poland alone had 2,269 at the end of 2019.

citations.note: Free-ranging herds named in the article, all from captive stock, plus herds introduced to Moldova, Spain, Denmark, the Czech Republic and Portugal. Free-ranging herds are shown as reintroduced; the five later herds as introduced, the article's word. Kyrgyzstan's origin is not explained.

media.altText: A European bison bull standing on grass

editorial.overview: A wild goat with long backward-curving horns found only in the northern mountains of Ethiopia, chiefly the Simien Mountains. It lives in mountain forest, subalpine grassland and scrub. Numbers fell to 200 to 250 in the mid-1990s and had recovered to about 500 by 2004. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Bushes, herbs, lichens, shrubs, grasses and creepers.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: About 500 individuals in 2004, up from 200 to 250 in 1994 to 1996.

citations.note: Endemic to the northern mountains of Ethiopia.

media.altText: A Walia ibex with long curved horns on rocky ground

editorial.overview: An egg-laying, semi-aquatic mammal of eastern Australia and Tasmania, with a duck-like bill, dense brown fur and venomous spurs on the males' hind legs. Underwater it closes its eyes, ears and nose and finds prey by sensing the tiny electric currents of their muscles. Hunted for fur until protected in 1912, it is now at risk from pollution, fishing bycatch and climate change. It is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Insect larvae, worms, shrimp, crayfish, freshwater mussels, tadpoles and fish eggs, dug from stream beds with its bill and stored in cheek pouches. Adults have grinding pads instead of teeth.

population.note: No population total in the source.

citations.note: Eastern Australia including Tasmania, with an introduced population on Kangaroo Island.

media.altText: A platypus with a duck-like bill swimming at the water surface

editorial.overview: A large, dark eagle that breeds from east-central and southeastern Europe across southern Russia and Central Asia to northwestern China and Mongolia. It prefers the edges of tall woods next to plains and steppe. Most birds migrate to winter in northeast Africa, the Middle East and southern and eastern Asia. Its small global population is declining. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An opportunist that mostly takes small mammals such as ground squirrels, but also many birds (over 120 species recorded), reptiles and other prey, almost always caught on the ground. In winter it can live largely on carrion.

population.note: No population figure in the source; it describes the global population as small and declining.

citations.note: Breeding countries as listed in the article, isolated populations in Cyprus, Turkey and northern Iran, and the main wintering areas named. Extirpated as a breeder in Greece; probably locally extinct in Afghanistan and Pakistan. Vagrant and scattered winter records are left out.

media.altText: An eastern imperial eagle standing on open ground

editorial.overview: One of the largest eagles in the world and the top predator of lowland tropical rainforest canopies from southern Mexico to northern Argentina. It has the largest talons of any living eagle and can carry prey of about half its own weight. Forest loss and shooting have made it nearly extinct in much of Central America. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Tree-dwelling mammals snatched from branches, especially sloths and monkeys (about a third of prey remains at some nests), plus other animals such as iguanas.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Southern Mexico to northern Argentina; countries are those the article names, so the list is partial. Gone from El Salvador and nearly so from Costa Rica. Belize birds include captive-bred releases.

media.altText: A harpy eagle flying with its wings spread

editorial.overview: A small Old World vulture of sub-Saharan Africa that is unafraid of people and often gathers around towns, rubbish dumps and abattoirs. It lives in grassland, wooded savanna, forest edges, deserts and coasts. Apart from stable pockets such as The Gambia, it has declined by an average of 83% over 53 years, mostly through poisoning and hunting. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A versatile scavenger of carcasses and human waste; it also feeds on insects, gathering in large numbers when termites emerge.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Total population estimated at a maximum of 197,000 individuals.

citations.note: Countries as listed in the article for West, East and southern Africa; the list is partial for a range across sub-Saharan Africa.

media.altText: A hooded vulture with a bare pink face perched on a dead branch

editorial.overview: The most widespread and common vulture in Africa, found from Senegal across the Sahel to Ethiopia and Somalia and south through East Africa to South Africa. It nests in tall trees, often acacias along rivers, in wooded savanna. Its numbers have dropped rapidly in recent years. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An obligate scavenger of large grazing mammals' carcasses. Its medium-sized beak cannot tear tough hide, so it eats soft tissues such as the innards, and it finds food by watching other vultures and carnivores.

population.note: No total in the source; it reports steep local declines, e.g. from 73 to 22 nesting pairs in one Botswana study area between 2007 and 2017.

citations.note: Countries the article names; Sahel and East African countries between them are not named and are left out.

media.altText: White-backed vultures on a dead tree, one with wings spread

editorial.overview: A vulture of the Indian subcontinent that breeds on small cliffs and crags, mostly in central and southern India. Its population collapsed in the 1990s and 2000s after vultures ate carcasses of cattle treated with the painkiller diclofenac, which causes kidney failure. India, Pakistan and Nepal banned the veterinary drug in 2006. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A scavenger, mostly of dead cattle and leftovers from large predators.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Estimated 5,000 to 15,000 mature individuals in the wild.

citations.note: Mostly central and peninsular India, also southwest Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal. Extinct in Southeast Asia (former range to Indochina and the northern Malay Peninsula).

media.altText: Indian vultures at a nest on a rocky ledge

editorial.overview: A tall, long-legged bird of prey found only in Africa, which spends most of its time walking on the ground. It lives in open grassland, savanna and shrubland from Senegal to Somalia and south to the Western Cape. It kills prey by stamping on it. Local surveys suggest a rapid decline, though it is thinly spread over a large range. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Insects and small vertebrates caught on foot: rodents, frogs, lizards, small tortoises, eggs and small birds. Snakes, including adders and cobras, can be locally important, though their role has been exaggerated.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Estimated in 2016 at between 6,700 and 67,000 individuals.

citations.note: From Senegal to Somalia and south to South Africa. Only a few countries in between are named in the article, so the list is partial.

media.altText: A secretarybird with long legs and a crest of black feathers in tall grass

editorial.overview: A large crane of sub-Saharan Africa with grey plumage, white cheeks, a red throat patch and a stiff golden crown. It lives in dry savanna but nests in wetter places, and is also found in marshes, farmland and grassy flats near rivers and lakes. It is the national bird of Uganda and appears on its flag. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore: plants, seeds, grain, insects, frogs, worms, snakes, small fish and the eggs of aquatic animals. It stamps its feet to flush insects and follows grazing antelopes to catch what they disturb.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Global population estimated at 58,000 to 77,000 individuals.

citations.note: East African subspecies from eastern DR Congo, Uganda and Kenya to eastern South Africa; the southern subspecies breeds from Angola to South Africa. Countries in between are not named in the article.

media.altText: A grey crowned crane with a golden crest of feathers

editorial.overview: A white starling with black wing tips and a patch of bright blue bare skin around the eye. It is found only in northwest Bali and nearby islands, where it is the island's only endemic vertebrate. Trapping for the cage-bird trade brought it close to extinction in the wild; captive breeding and releases have created new populations, including on Nusa Penida. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Fruit, seeds, worms and insects.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: In 2020 fewer than 50 adults were assumed to exist in the wild; about 1,000 live in captivity.

citations.note: Endemic to Bali, Indonesia: West Bali National Park, Nusa Penida and nearby islands.

media.altText: A white Bali myna with blue skin around its eye, perched on a twig

editorial.overview: A medium-sized white cockatoo with a yellow crest, from wooded and farmed land on Sulawesi, the Lesser Sundas and East Timor. Illegal trapping for the cage-bird trade and logging, especially of mangroves and kapok trees, have caused a dramatic decline. A feral population lives in Hong Kong. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly seeds, buds, fruit, nuts and herbaceous plants.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Estimated at fewer than 2,500 individuals and thought to be declining.

citations.note: Sulawesi and the Lesser Sunda Islands (Indonesia) and East Timor. The introduced Hong Kong population is not mapped.

media.altText: A white yellow-crested cockatoo with its crest raised

editorial.overview: A large green macaw of wet tropical forest in the Atlantic lowlands of Central America, from Honduras to Panama and Colombia, with a separate subspecies in the dry forests of western Ecuador. In Costa Rica it depends heavily on the almendro tree for food and nest holes. Habitat loss has been the main threat, and reintroduction projects are under way. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Seeds, nuts and fruit, and also flowers, bulbs, roots and bark. In Costa Rica it uses at least 38 food plants, the most important being almendro nuts; flocks move to follow ripening fruit.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: 500 to 1,000 mature individuals, as given by the IUCN's 2020 assessment cited in the article.

citations.note: Atlantic lowlands from Honduras to Panama and Colombia; Pacific lowlands of Panama, Colombia and western Ecuador.

media.altText: A great green macaw with green plumage and a reddish forehead among leaves

editorial.overview: A grey African parrot with a red tail, famous for its skill at mimicking sounds and speech. It lives in dense equatorial forest, forest edges and gallery forest from Côte d'Ivoire to Kenya. Trapping for the pet trade, along with logging and hunting, has devastated some populations: it has been almost wiped out in Ghana. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly fruit, nuts and seeds, including oil palm fruit, and sometimes flowers, bark, insects and snails. It partly feeds on the ground.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Global estimates are uncertain and range from 630,000 to 13 million birds.

citations.note: Equatorial Africa from Côte d'Ivoire to Kenya and Tanzania, with Bioko (Equatorial Guinea); Príncipe and São Tomé are too small for our map. Virtually eliminated from Ghana.

media.altText: A grey parrot with grey feathers perched on a branch

editorial.overview: A huge seabird with the longest wingspan of any living bird, up to 3.7 m. It spends most of its life in flight over the Southern Ocean, landing only to breed and feed; some birds circle the Southern Ocean three times in a year. It breeds on sub-Antarctic islands. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Squid and other cephalopods, small fish and crustaceans, taken at the surface by day. It also follows fishing boats for bait, catch and offal.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: All southern oceans between 28° and 60°S. Breeds on South Georgia (not on our map), the Crozet and Kerguelen Islands (French Southern Lands), the Prince Edward Islands (South Africa) and Macquarie Island (Australia); feeds year-round off Kaikōura, New Zealand.

media.altText: A wandering albatross resting on the sea

editorial.overview: A large, rare albatross of the North Pacific with a big pink bill. It was hunted on an industrial scale for its feathers in the late 19th century, possibly more than 10 million birds, and was declared extinct in 1949 before survivors were found. Protected since the 1950s, it now breeds on a few islands, mostly Tori-shima off Japan. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly squid; it also follows ships for discarded offal.

population.note: No current population figure in the source.

citations.note: Breeds mainly on Tori-shima (Japan) and in the Senkaku Islands, with a few pairs in the Bonin Islands and on Midway (Hawaii, USA); ranges across the North Pacific outside the breeding season.

media.altText: A dark-plumaged short-tailed albatross with a pink bill standing on a shore

editorial.overview: A medium-sized penguin of the Pacific coast of Peru and Chile, living where the cold, food-rich Humboldt Current flows. It nests on islands and rocky coasts, often burrowing into old guano. Guano harvesting in the 1800s destroyed many nesting sites, and El Niño events, overfishing, fishing nets, oil spills and bird flu have hit it since. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly schooling fish caught near the surface, such as anchovy, Araucanian herring and silversides in the south and saury and garfish in the north, plus some squid and crustaceans. Spines on its tongue help it hold prey.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Roughly 23,800 mature individuals and declining.

citations.note: Pacific coast of Peru and Chile; vagrant in Ecuador and Colombia.

media.altText: A Humboldt penguin, head and upper body

editorial.overview: A penguin found only in New Zealand, known in Māori as hoiho, and the only living member of its genus. It breeds on the east and southeast coasts of the South Island, Stewart Island and the subantarctic Auckland and Campbell Islands. The mainland population has collapsed in recent decades through disease, warming seas, fishing and predators. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: About 90% fish, mostly species living near the seabed such as silversides, plus some crustaceans including krill.

population.note: No total in the source; it reports mainland breeding pairs falling from 739 to 143 since 2008, and about 577 pairs a year on Enderby Island.

citations.note: Endemic to New Zealand, including its subantarctic islands.

media.altText: Two yellow-eyed penguins with pale yellow head bands and a chick

editorial.overview: A nocturnal, flightless kiwi of the northern two-thirds of New Zealand's North Island and nearby islands. Females are larger than males, and its eggs are among the largest of any bird relative to body size. Introduced predators such as dogs, cats, stoats and ferrets, along with forest clearance, have cut its numbers by at least 90% since 1900. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly invertebrates such as worms and spiders (85 to 95% of its food), plus plant matter, found by smell and touch on the forest floor at night.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: About 26,600 in 2015, of which 10,000 to 19,999 mature individuals.

citations.note: North Island of New Zealand and adjacent islands.

media.altText: A North Island brown kiwi with a long bill on the forest floor

editorial.overview: One of the larger hornbills, with a bright yellow and black casque on top of its massive bill. It lives in dense old-growth forest in hilly country in India, Bhutan, Nepal, mainland Southeast Asia, Sumatra and western Java, and is an important spreader of forest tree seeds. Deforestation and hunting for its meat, casque and feathers are its main threats. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly fruit, especially figs and fat-rich fruits of the laurel and nutmeg families, from which it gets all its water. It also catches small mammals, reptiles and birds.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: India, Bhutan, Nepal, mainland Southeast Asia, Sumatra and Ujung Kulon in Java. The mainland Southeast Asian countries are inferred from that phrase, not named one by one.

media.altText: A great hornbill in flight carrying food in its bill

editorial.overview: A heavy bird of open grassland, steppe and farmland, and the only living member of its genus. It breeds from northern Morocco through southern and central Europe to Central and East Asia. Steep declines have left more than half the world population in central Spain; small populations in Germany and Austria have been growing for two decades. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore whose diet changes with the season: green plants such as alfalfa, legumes and dandelion, seeds of wheat and barley, grapes, and invertebrates. In winter it eats almost only seeds and green plants.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Global population as of 2008, about 38,000 to 47,000 of them in Europe.

citations.note: Countries the article names with populations; birds breeding in northern Mongolia winter in Shaanxi, China. In Iran only 19 birds were counted in January 2025.

media.altText: A great bustard walking in a grassy field

editorial.overview: A large bustard of the Indian subcontinent with a horizontal body and long bare legs. Once common on dry grasslands and scrub in India and Pakistan, it has been wiped out from 90% of its former range by hunting and habitat loss. The last populations are mainly in Desert National Park near Jaisalmer and the grasslands of Kutch. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore: grass seeds, berries, insects, rodents and reptiles such as spiny-tailed lizards. In farmland it also eats groundnuts, millets and legume pods.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: As few as 150 were estimated to survive in 2018, down from about 250 in 2008.

citations.note: India (Rajasthan and Gujarat). A few birds were detected in Pakistan's Cholistan Desert in 2013.

media.altText: A great Indian bustard with a black crown and pale neck in dry grass

editorial.overview: A tiny wader with a spoon-shaped bill tip that it sweeps from side to side as it feeds. It breeds on coastal tundra of the Chukchi Peninsula and Kamchatka in Russia and migrates down the Pacific coast to winter in South and Southeast Asia. Loss of tidal flats along its flyway and trapping on its wintering grounds have caused a steep decline. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: On the tundra, insects such as mosquitoes, flies and beetles, spiders and some moss; on the coast, marine invertebrates such as shrimp and worms.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Global estimate as of 2016: 240 to 456 mature individuals, at most 228 pairs.

citations.note: Breeds in northeastern Russia; passes through Japan, Korea and China; winter records from the countries listed in the article (Singapore is too small for our map).

media.altText: A spoon-billed sandpiper standing on dry grass

editorial.overview: An ibis that was once widespread across eastern China, Korea and Japan. Overhunting, pesticides and habitat loss reduced the wild population by the late 20th century to one site at Yangxian in Shaanxi, China. Captive breeding and reintroductions have since re-established it in South Korea and on Japan's Sado Island and Noto Peninsula. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Small fish and loaches, frogs, crabs, shrimp, snails, earthworms and insects, caught by day in shallow water, rice paddies and mud.

population.note: No current wild total in the source.

citations.note: Wild population in Shaanxi, China; reintroduced in Japan and South Korea. It formerly also nested in the Russian Far East and visited Taiwan in winter.

media.altText: A crested ibis with a red face standing in a green field

editorial.overview: One of the largest flying birds in the world, with a wingspan of up to 3.3 m and a weight of up to 15 kg. It lives along the Andes and the adjacent Pacific coast, soaring over open grassland and mountains up to 5,000 m and nesting on inaccessible rock ledges. It is a national symbol of Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly a scavenger of carrion, which it spots from the air in open country, travelling more than 200 km a day. It occasionally catches small live animals such as rodents, birds and rabbits.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Only about 10,000 individuals remain, as stated in the source.

citations.note: Along the Andes from Venezuela and Colombia (extremely rare there) to Tierra del Fuego. It occasionally reaches lowlands in southwestern Brazil.

media.altText: An Andean condor soaring with wings spread over a canyon

editorial.overview: A peafowl of the tropical forests of Southeast Asia and southern China and the national bird of Myanmar. It was once common from Yunnan and northeast India through Indochina to Peninsular Malaysia and Java. Deforestation, farming and hunting for meat, feathers and the pet trade have left only isolated populations, notably in Cambodia, adjacent Vietnam and protected areas of Java. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Wild population estimated at about 5,000 to 10,000 around 1995. Keo Seima in Cambodia held about 745 in 2020.

citations.note: Surviving populations named in Cambodia, adjacent Vietnam and Java (Indonesia). The other countries are its former range; the article does not say whether birds remain there, and Indian records are questioned.

media.altText: Green peafowl on the ground, one with a long train

editorial.overview: A large falcon that breeds from central Europe east across the Palearctic to Manchuria, in open grassland with some trees or cliffs. It hunts by fast horizontal chases at 120 to 150 km/h. It is the national bird of Hungary, the United Arab Emirates and Mongolia. Illegal trapping on migration and habitat loss have contributed to a rapid decline, worst in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly rodents and birds; in Europe ground squirrels and feral pigeons are the commonest prey.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Estimated at 7,200 to 8,800 mature individuals in 2004.

citations.note: Countries the article names within a range from central Europe to Manchuria; the list is partial. Migrants cross the Middle East, Arabia and Pakistan.

media.altText: A saker falcon in flight

editorial.overview: A small Old World vulture with white plumage that often looks rusty from mud and soil, found from the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa to West Asia and India. It is one of the few birds known to use tools: it breaks large eggs by throwing pebbles at them. Its numbers have fallen in most of its range, by 35% a year in India between 1999 and 2003. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly carrion, but also faeces, insects in dung, plant matter, eggs and small mammals, birds and reptiles. It is the only Old World vulture that regularly eats faeces.

population.note: No global figure in the source; it gives regional counts, e.g. about 130 birds in the Canary Islands in 2000.

citations.note: Countries named in the article within a range from Iberia and North Africa to India; the list is partial. Once bred in South Africa's Transkei, before 1923.

media.altText: An Egyptian vulture with pale plumage

editorial.overview: A very large stork with a bare head and a hanging neck pouch. It was once widespread across southern and Southeast Asia, but now has only three breeding populations: two in India (Assam and around Bhagalpur) and one in Cambodia. Locally called hargila, the bone-swallower, it stalks shallow lakes, drying lake beds and rubbish dumps. Its small population now appears to be growing. It is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List (2025.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly carrion and offal, soaring with vultures to find it; it also catches vertebrates.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: World population estimated at 1,360 to 1,510 mature individuals as of 2023; appears to be increasing.

citations.note: Extant in India and Cambodia; probably extinct in Bangladesh, Laos, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan, Thailand and Vietnam (IUCN, as cited in the article).

media.altText: Two greater adjutant storks standing on a rubbish dump

editorial.overview: A small, brilliantly coloured bird of montane cloud forest from southern Mexico to western Panama; males grow tail streamers up to a metre long. It moves up and down the mountains with the seasons. It is the national animal of Guatemala and gives its name to the country's currency. It is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A fruit specialist, eating 41 to 43 kinds of fruit, over half of them from the laurel family, including wild avocados. It also takes insects such as wasps, ants and larvae, which are the main food of chicks.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Estimated population of 20,000 to 49,999 individuals, as cited from the IUCN in the article.

citations.note: Southern Mexico (Oaxaca, Chiapas) to western Panama (Chiriquí).

media.altText: A male resplendent quetzal with a red belly and long green tail feathers on a branch

editorial.overview: A medium-sized freshwater crocodile of mainland Southeast Asia and Indonesian Borneo, and one of the most endangered crocodiles. Its global population has fallen by over 80% since the 1940s. It lives in slow rivers, lakes, oxbows and marshes up to 730 m, and is being pushed to the edges of its former range by farming, pesticides and dams on the Mekong. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Adults eat mainly fish and snakes, along with amphibians and small mammals.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Cambodian population, from surveys between 2000 and 2014. No global total in the source.

citations.note: Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam. As of 2012, possibly extinct in Indonesia (Kalimantan) and uncertain in Myanmar and Malaysia.

media.altText: A Siamese crocodile resting beside water

editorial.overview: A freshwater crocodilian with a very long, slender snout, living in peat swamps and lowland swamp forest of Peninsular Malaysia, Borneo and Sumatra. Draining of swamps for plantations, logging, fires and hunting for skin, meat and eggs have shrunk its range; it is locally extinct in Java and Thailand. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A generalist: fish and smaller aquatic animals, and in large adults also bigger prey such as proboscis monkeys, long-tailed macaques, deer and waterbirds.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Global population estimated at around 2,500 to 10,000 mature individuals; the article also cites fewer than 2,500 as of 2010.

citations.note: Peninsular Malaysia, Borneo and Sumatra; Brunei is on Borneo but not named, so it is marked uncertain. Locally extinct in Java and Thailand.

media.altText: A false gharial with a long thin snout resting on a rock

editorial.overview: A small to medium crocodile found only in Cuba, typically 2.1 to 2.3 m long. Fossils show it once lived across the Caribbean, but hunting has confined it to Cuba's Zapata Swamp. Captive animals hunt cooperatively, and hybridisation with the American crocodile is a serious threat. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Adults eat mainly small mammals, fish and turtles, crushing shells with blunt rear teeth; young eat small fish, arthropods and crustaceans.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Endemic to Cuba; fossils come from the Bahamas, Hispaniola and the Cayman Islands.

media.altText: A Cuban crocodile with speckled scales in shallow muddy water

editorial.overview: One of the largest lizards in the Caribbean, with a thick tail and spiked jowls. It lives across mainland Cuba and its islets, with a subspecies on Little Cayman and Cayman Brac. A strong swimmer, it escapes into water when threatened. Feral cats are a main threat. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly plants: purslane, prickly pear, black mangrove, cacti and grasses, plus fruit and flowers. It occasionally scavenges dead birds, fish and crabs.

population.note: No total in the source; it gives local counts such as 2,000 to 3,000 at Guantánamo Bay and about 1,500 on Little Cayman.

citations.note: Cuba and its islets, and the Cayman Islands (Little Cayman and Cayman Brac; not on our map). A feral population lives on Isla Magueyes, Puerto Rico.

media.altText: A Cuban rock iguana on rocky ground

editorial.overview: A tree-dwelling iguana found only in the Lau Islands of eastern Fiji, from Vanua Balavu in the north to Fulaga and Ogea in the south. Its ancestors are thought to have rafted about 9,000 km across the Pacific from the Americas. Habitat loss to fire, storms, farming and feral goats, and introduced rats, mongooses and cats, have reduced its numbers. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A plant eater: leaves, fruit and flowers of trees and shrubs, especially hibiscus flowers. Captive hatchlings eat insects, but adults usually do not.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Endemic to the Lau Islands of Fiji.

media.altText: A green Fiji banded iguana with pale bands on a branch

editorial.overview: The smallest and rarest sea turtle, and the most endangered. Adults live mainly in shallow waters of the Gulf of Mexico, and most females return each year to one beach, Rancho Nuevo in Tamaulipas, Mexico, to nest in mass gatherings during the day. Egg collecting and poaching first depleted it; shrimp nets, pollution, oil spills and habitat loss threaten it today. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Adults feed on the bottom, mainly on crabs, plus other crustaceans, molluscs, jellyfish, fish, sea urchins and seaweed. Juveniles feed at the surface in open water.

population.note: No population count in the source; nesting in 2016 was estimated at 9.9% of the 1947 level.

citations.note: Gulf of Mexico, nesting mainly in Tamaulipas and Veracruz (Mexico) and Texas (USA). Juveniles wander into the North Atlantic; vagrants reach Europe and the Mediterranean.

media.altText: A Kemp's ridley sea turtle on a sandy beach

editorial.overview: The second-smallest and most abundant sea turtle, found in warm and tropical waters, mainly of the Pacific and Indian Oceans. It is known for arribadas, synchronised mass nestings when thousands of females come ashore together, in places such as Mexico, Costa Rica, Nicaragua and eastern India. Despite its numbers it has declined by more than 30% from historic levels. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly carnivorous: salps and sea squirts, starfish, sea urchins, squid, snails, bivalves, barnacles, shrimp, crabs and fish, and algae where little else is available.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Annual nesting females worldwide in 2008, down from about two million in 2004.

citations.note: Oceans as described in the article; countries are main nesting or coastal areas named in it, so the list is partial.

media.altText: An olive ridley sea turtle on a sandy beach

editorial.overview: One of the largest lizards in the world, 0.9 to 1.5 m long, living in the dry lowlands of several Galápagos islands, including Fernandina, Isabela and Santa Cruz. Introduced pigs, rats, cats and dogs wiped out whole populations, including all the iguanas on Santiago Island; relocations have helped others recover. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly plants, especially prickly-pear cactus, which also provides most of its water; some individuals also eat animal food opportunistically.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Estimated 5,000 to 10,000 across the Galápagos Islands.

citations.note: Endemic to the Galápagos Islands, Ecuador.

media.altText: A Galápagos land iguana, close-up of its head

editorial.overview: A small true toad that once ranged along mountain streams from Costa Rica into western Panama. Climate shifts and the spread of the chytrid fungus wiped out most populations from around 1990. It now survives as one remnant population near Quepos, Costa Rica, rediscovered in 2003, and relict populations in western Panama. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Small arthropods, which are most plentiful in the dry season.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Costa Rica (near Quepos) and western Panama.

media.altText: A variable harlequin toad with black and yellow markings

editorial.overview: A true frog found only in California, in the San Jacinto, San Bernardino and San Gabriel mountains and the southern Sierra Nevada. It lives in sunny mountain creeks, lakes and pools, and its tadpoles need permanent water for at least two years. It has declined by about 98% because of introduced trout, chytrid fungus, livestock grazing and pesticide drift. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Aquatic insects and other invertebrates of the stream or lake bed; in streams it also eats land insects such as beetles, ants, bees, flies and dragonflies, and the larvae of other frogs and toads.

population.note: No count in the source; it reports a 98% decline, with remaining populations at fewer than 10 sites.

citations.note: Endemic to California, USA.

media.altText: A mountain yellow-legged frog in shallow water

editorial.overview: A small frog, uniformly yellow, orange or red, found only in Madagascar, in three small areas around the town of Moramanga, including the Torotorofotsy wetland near Andasibe. Its colour warns predators that its skin is poisonous; the toxins come from its food. It is one of Madagascar's most threatened amphibians because of heavy human pressure on its tiny range and collection for the pet trade. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Small invertebrates, from which it gets its skin toxins.

population.note: No population figure in the source; it describes the population as decreasing.

citations.note: Endemic to Madagascar, around Moramanga.

media.altText: A small orange golden mantella frog on a person's palm

editorial.overview: A secretive frog of the Gulf Coastal Plain of the United States that covers its eyes with its hands when exposed to light or threatened. It was once common in Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama, but the loss of open longleaf pine forest and seasonal breeding ponds left it at a few ponds in coastal Mississippi.
