Intensive work has raised the population to around 600 adults. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Adults probably eat frogs, toads, insects, spiders and earthworms.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Numbers have grown to around 600 adults after intensive conservation work.

citations.note: Coastal Mississippi, USA (formerly also Louisiana and Alabama).

media.altText: A dark, warty Mississippi gopher frog

editorial.overview: A large sturgeon that lives in coastal seas and migrates up rivers to breed. It was once common along the coasts of Europe and caught heavily for caviar until the early 20th century. It now breeds only in France's Garonne river basin, where it last hatched naturally in 1994; captive-bred fish have been released into the Gironde estuary and Germany's Elbe. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Polychaete worms and crustaceans, found on the bottom with its barbels.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Estimated 20 to 750 mature individuals in the wild at the 2020 assessment.

citations.note: Breeds only in the Garonne basin, France; restocked fish in the Gironde estuary and the Elbe (Germany). The sea range is not described country by country.

media.altText: A European sea sturgeon

editorial.overview: A large requiem shark of the open ocean in tropical and warm temperate seas. It usually stays in the top 150 m of water over deep ocean, far from land. Once extremely common, it has been devastated by fishing, mostly as bycatch and for its fins and meat, and is estimated to have declined by around 98%. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly squid and other open-ocean cephalopods and bony fish such as tuna, barracuda and dolphinfish, but also stingrays, sea turtles, seabirds, crustaceans and carrion.

population.note: Total global population unknown; declines of around 98% are estimated.

citations.note: Worldwide in tropical and warm temperate open ocean; seas named in the article are added.

media.altText: An oceanic whitetip shark swimming with small pilot fish

editorial.overview: The fastest known shark, reaching about 50 km/h with bursts up to 74 km/h, found offshore in temperate and tropical seas worldwide. It hunts by lunging up from below and tearing chunks from its prey. It is targeted by sport and commercial fisheries and caught as bycatch, and was uplisted to Endangered in 2019. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly squid and other cephalopods and bony fish such as bluefish and swordfish.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Worldwide in offshore temperate and tropical seas.

media.altText: A shortfin mako shark swimming in blue water

editorial.overview: The largest hammerhead shark, found in warm waters around the world, from coral reefs and lagoons to continental shelves. It uses its wide head to sense prey and to pin stingrays to the sea floor. Heavy fishing for its valuable fins and very high mortality as bycatch have caused large declines worldwide. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A varied diet: crabs, lobsters, squid and octopus, bony fish such as tarpon and sardines, and other sharks and rays, especially stingrays.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Warm waters worldwide: the Atlantic from North Carolina to Uruguay and from Morocco to Senegal and the Mediterranean, the rim of the Indian Ocean and the Pacific from the Ryukyus to Australia and French Polynesia.

media.altText: A great hammerhead shark seen from below

editorial.overview: A rare, heavy-bodied ray with a shark-like body, found near the sea floor in tropical coastal waters of the western Indo-Pacific, down to 90 m. Thorns on its head and back protect it. It is caught throughout its range by trawls and gillnets, for its fins and meat, and is also harmed by blast fishing, coral bleaching and silt. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly bottom-living bony fish such as croakers, and crabs and shrimp, crushed with bands of flattened teeth; also bivalves and cephalopods.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Western Indo-Pacific from KwaZulu-Natal and the Red Sea across South and Southeast Asia to Australia, north to Korea and southern Japan and east to New Guinea. Countries are those named in the article.

media.altText: A bowmouth guitarfish with shark-like fins in an aquarium

editorial.overview: A long freshwater fish of Southeast Asia, in several colour varieties, that lives in blackwater rivers and slow waters through forested swamps and wetlands. It is highly prized as an aquarium fish, especially in places influenced by Chinese culture, and red and gold varieties are rarest. Habitat loss is probably a greater threat than collection. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Adults eat other fish and juveniles eat insects; it feeds at night near the surface.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Green variety in Indonesia (Kalimantan and Sumatra), Vietnam, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Malaysia; red variety only in the upper Kapuas River, Borneo.

media.altText: An Asian arowana of a red-orange variety with large shining scales

editorial.overview: One of the largest freshwater fish in the world; a 2005 catch set the Guinness record for the largest freshwater fish. Grey to white and toothless, it lives mainly in the deep main channel of the Mekong. Its range once spanned almost the whole 4,800 km river from Vietnam to Yunnan, but overfishing and habitat loss have removed it from most of that. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Young fish eat zooplankton; after about a year it becomes a plant eater, grazing algae from submerged rocks.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: The Mekong in Cambodia, Thailand and Laos. Vietnam and Yunnan (China) are its historical range ends; the article says it is gone from most of its former range.

media.altText: A Mekong giant catfish, a large grey fish, in an aquarium

editorial.overview: One of the largest groupers, living on rocky reefs, wrecks, artificial reefs and oil platforms in the western Atlantic from Florida to Brazil, the eastern Pacific from Mexico to Peru and West Africa from Senegal southward. Young fish grow up in mangroves. Because it gathers in small spawning groups, it is very vulnerable to overfishing. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Slow-moving fish such as stingrays, catfish, toadfish, burrfish and cowfish, and crustaceans; occasionally octopus and young sea turtles.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Florida to Brazil including the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean; Mexico to Peru in the eastern Pacific; Senegal to Cabinda in West Africa. Only end-point countries are named in the article.

media.altText: An Atlantic goliath grouper, a very large mottled fish, near a reef

editorial.overview: A tiny pupfish found only in Devils Hole, a water-filled cavern in the Amargosa Desert of southwestern Nevada, possibly the smallest habitat holding the entire population of any vertebrate. It feeds and spawns on one small, shallow rock shelf. Groundwater pumping in the 1960s and 1970s lowered the water and nearly wiped it out; counts fell to 35 in 2013 before recovering. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Almost every food available in Devils Hole, including algae, beetles, snails and small freshwater crustaceans, varying by season.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: 263 fish were counted in September 2022; counts have not exceeded about 550 since 1972.

citations.note: Devils Hole, Nevada, USA.

media.altText: Devils Hole pupfish, small blue fish, swimming over rock

editorial.overview: One of the largest bony fish in the world, up to 3.3 m long and 2,300 kg, with a tall, flattened body. It lives in temperate and tropical waters of every ocean and often basks on its side at the surface, where birds pick parasites from its skin. Females can produce up to 300 million eggs at once, more than any other known vertebrate. Its main threat is drift gillnets. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A generalist predator: once thought to eat mainly jellyfish, it mostly eats small fish, fish larvae, squid and other molluscs as well as jellyfish from the surface down to the seabed.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Temperate and tropical waters of every ocean.

media.altText: An ocean sunfish with a tall, flat body swimming

editorial.overview: A small air-breathing land snail found only in the Waianae Range of Oahu, Hawaii, in dry, wet and mesic forest at 600 to 1,158 m. It is slow to mature, at about seven years, and can live 15 to 20 years. Invasive predators, especially the predatory snail Euglandina rosea and introduced chameleons, are driving its decline. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Grazes at night on fungus growing on the surface of leaves.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Endemic to the Waianae Range, Oahu, Hawaii (USA).

media.altText: An Oahu tree snail with a banded shell on a leaf

editorial.overview: A marine arthropod more closely related to spiders than to crabs, found along the Atlantic coast of the United States from Maine to Florida, in the Gulf of Mexico and on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. Its eggs, laid on beaches such as Delaware Bay, are an important food for shorebirds. It is caught for fishing bait and for its blood, used in a test for bacterial toxins, and is losing habitat. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Molluscs, worms and other bottom-living invertebrates, plus bits of fish, ground up with bristles on its legs and a gizzard full of sand and gravel.

population.note: No population total in the source; some populations are rising, some stable and some declining.

citations.note: Atlantic coast of the USA (Maine to Florida), the Gulf of Mexico and Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, its only breeding population outside the USA.

media.altText: An Atlantic horseshoe crab with a domed brown shell

editorial.overview: A horseshoe crab of East and Southeast Asia that lives in coastal sea and brackish water and copes with colder water than other Asian horseshoe crabs. It needs shallow sandy or muddy shores near mangroves and mudflats to spawn and grow. Overfishing, pollution, sand mining and coastal development have caused declines for decades; Japan protected it in 1928. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore: molluscs, worms, other bottom-living invertebrates and algae. Juveniles feed on exposed mud at low tide.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Countries with records as listed in the article.

media.altText: Tri-spine horseshoe crabs in a tank

editorial.overview: A fast-growing branching stony coral with thick, upright antler-like branches, once one of the most important reef builders of the western Atlantic, from the Florida Keys and the Bahamas to the Caribbean islands. Dense thickets covered many fore reefs until the late 1970s; since then white-band disease and human pressures have cut its cover by over 95% in some areas. After the 2023 marine heatwave it is functionally extinct on Florida's reefs. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Gets most of its energy from symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) in its tissues, and at night its polyps catch passing zooplankton with stinging tentacles.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Florida Keys, the Bahamas and the Caribbean islands, and the western Gulf of Mexico (absent from US Gulf waters). Individual Caribbean islands are not listed.
